text.text: Event costs
Most lost catering business is lost in the first 48 hours. Answer fast, ask the right questions, and send a proposal the client can say yes to.
The first call
Date, time, venue and whether it has a kitchen
Guest count and the kind of event
Service style: plated, buffet, family style, stations or drop-off
Budget per guest, and what must be included (bar, rentals, staff)
Dietary needs and allergies
Proposal within two working days
Add the event as
Inquiry
, then build the menu from your dishes.
Price per guest from the menu prices, adjusted for style: plated needs more staff than a buffet.
Add the service charge and state what it covers.
Send it and set
Proposal sent
. Follow up after three days.
What a good proposal says

cells.text: Dishes by course, with dietary marks
Style, staff count, hours on site
Per guest, service charge, tax, deposit and balance dates
Arrival time, kitchen needs, rentals, cleanup
Final count date, cancellation, what happens if the count drops

text.text: Signing
Contract signed by the client
Deposit received; enter it on the event
Status set to
Booked
Final count date entered, usually 7 to 14 days before
Tasting booked for weddings and large dinners
Deposits and payment

Most caterers take 30 to 50 percent to hold the date and the balance a few days before the event. Corporate clients often pay on invoice after the event; agree that in writing and note it on the event so nobody chases a deposit that was never due.
Final count
On the final count date, confirm guests and dietary counts in writing. The count can go up after this date, rarely down. Update guests on the event and the portions on every prep item.
Example
The Chamber mixer proposal is out for 90 guests at stations, 52 dollars a head plus 20 percent service. The follow-up call is booked for later this week.
Off-site food must survive a van ride and still taste fresh. Prep week is planned backwards from the moment food leaves the kitchen.
The event order
The event order is the kitchen's copy of the event: menu, portions, dietary counts, service style, timings and venue notes. Send it to the kitchen a week out and tick
Event order sent to kitchen
Plan the prep
Add one prep item per dish per event, with portions and the cook.
Set the
prep date
: two days ahead for rillettes and dressings, one day for proteins and salads, the morning of for anything that wilts.
Plan oven and fridge space across all events that week, not one at a time.
Order ingredients from the combined prep list.
Statuses

cells.text: On the list, nobody has begun
Labeled, in its container, in the van fridge or staging area

text.text: Packing
Each container labeled with the event, dish, portions and allergens
Hot food in insulated carriers above 135 degrees Fahrenheit
Cold food at 41 degrees or below
Allergy-free meals packed separately and marked with the guest's name
Serving utensils, chafers, fuel, platters, linens, gloves, towels, trash bags
Printed event order and run of service
The day before
Walk the walk-in with the prep list in hand. Anything not Prepped by mid-afternoon gets a second cook. Check the van: fuel, clean fridge, straps, a spare tire.
Portions
Make 3 to 5 percent extra for buffets and stations; plated events get exact counts plus a few spares for vendors and mistakes. Never cut portions to cover a last-minute count change.
Example
The crostini for Cobalt should have been made earlier this week. The cook moves it to first thing in the morning, and the kitchen lead checks that the 170 pieces still fit the van's sheet-tray rack.
On the day, the captain runs the event. Everything they need should be on the event page and in the van.
Before leaving the kitchen
Pack list checked against the event order
Staff confirmed with call times
Venue contact, address, parking and load-in door
Weather plan for outdoor service
Cash or card reader for bar sales if agreed
On site
Arrive at the agreed time; walk the space with the venue contact.
Set the kitchen or staging area; check power for warmers.
Set the buffet, stations or tables to the plan.
Brief the staff: menu, allergies, timing, who to call.
Taste every hot dish before it goes out.
During service
The captain keeps the timeline and talks to the client's host.
Allergy plates go out first, by name, from a separate tray.
Track what runs short; never substitute a dish without telling the host.
Timing for a plated dinner

cells.text: Tables and bar set; staff briefing
Hot food warming; cold plates assembled

text.text: Breakdown
Leftovers handled as agreed with the client, labeled and dated
Venue kitchen left as clean as found
Rentals counted and stacked for pickup
Damage or losses written down with photos
After the event
An event that has passed but is not marked Served shows under Overdue; it usually means the balance has not been invoiced. Set the event to
Served
. Note what ran short, what came back, how long setup took and any client feedback. Invoice the balance the next working day.
Example
The Cobalt board dinner needs a second server; that shift is still Requested. The captain confirms someone before the end of the week, and the call time is set for 4:30 pm on site.
One allergy mistake can hurt a guest and end a business. Treat dietary needs as part of the order, not a note in the margin.
Collect it early
Ask for allergies and dietary needs at the proposal and again at the final count.
Write the counts on the event: "12 vegetarian, 4 vegan, 2 nut allergies".
For plated events, ask for names and seat numbers of guests with allergies.
Mark every dish

Each dish on the menu carries its dietary mark: vegan, vegetarian, gluten free, contains nuts, contains dairy, contains shellfish. Recheck marks whenever a recipe changes, including garnishes and sauces.
In the kitchen
Allergy meals made first, with clean boards, knives and gloves
Packed in separate, labeled containers with the guest's name
Never use shared fryer oil for allergy-free food
Nuts and shellfish stored apart and below other food
Temperatures

cells.text: 135 to 70 within two hours, to 41 within four more

text.text: Probe and write down temperatures at packing, arrival and service.
Labels on the buffet
Small cards for every dish: name and dietary marks. Staff should know the ingredients of every dish and say "let me check" rather than guess.
Staff training

Every server learns the allergy routine in their first shift: how meals are marked, how to answer questions, and who to fetch when unsure. Repeat it at every pre-service briefing; it takes one minute.
When something goes wrong
Stop serving the dish.
Help the guest; call emergency services if there is any sign of a reaction.
Tell the client's host and the owner.
Write down what happened, the dish and the batch.
Example
The Kessler-Adeyemi wedding has one shellfish allergy. The smoked trout is fine, but the captain makes sure that guest's appetizer comes from a separate tray, and the place card is marked.
A catering business sells a promise months ahead and delivers it in a few hours somewhere else. This workspace keeps the promise, the kitchen work and the people in one place for every event.
The lists

Date, venue, style, guests and dietary counts, price per guest, service charge, deposit, balance, final count date, food and labor cost
Each dish with cost and price per guest, food cost percent, dietary notes
Each dish for each event: portions, prep date, cook, cost and container
Each shift: role, person, hours, rate, labor cost, call time

text.text: How the money works
Event total
is guests times price per guest. The
service charge
is a percentage on top.
Balance due
is total plus service charge, minus the deposit received.
Food cost
adds the prep items for the event: portions times cost per portion from the menu.
Labor cost
adds the staff shifts. Food plus labor against the event total shows what the event really earns.
Your first week
Enter the menu with cost and price per guest. Cost the five dishes you sell most first.
Add booked events with guests, price, deposit and final count date.
For events in the next two weeks, add prep items and staff shifts.
Note every allergy and dietary count on the event, not in an email.
The weekly rhythm
Monday:
events this week and next; final counts due; staff gaps under Shifts not confirmed.
Two days before:
prep list printed by day; containers chosen.
Event day:
pack list checked against the event order before the van leaves.
Example

Cobalt's all-hands lunch is a buffet for 85 with 12 vegetarian, 4 vegan and 2 nut allergies. The cake is packed, the chicken is prepped, and the crostini batch is late, so it is first on the list for the morning cook.
